newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac plugs euro, austerity, rules out reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Chirac plugs euro, austerity, rules out reshuffle.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, offering no miracle cures for gloom in France, has pledged to move on with austerity policies and European integration while ruling out a cabinet reshuffle.

In his first major interview since July, Chirac sought to persuade French citizens that France was on the right track and that he had not forgotten 1995 campaign promises such as a war on unemployment, which has since risen to a record 12.6 percent

But Chirac came under fire for offering little new in a two-hour teleivison interview on the eve of Friday's European Union summit in Dublin and for blaming the French people for being too resistant to change.
"Jacques Chirac...stuck to the course of a policy that doesn't work," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.

Chirac made a strong defence of a planned single European currency from 1999 and budget rigour needed to qualify for it, saying the euro was vital to revive France's sluggish economy and to give Europe the power to challenge U.S. "hegemony".

And he said a devaluation suggested by government allies including former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing would be disastrous -- saying it would break the Franco-German alliance at the heart of the European Union.
He said he believed the EU would reach agreement, perhaps during the Dublin summit, on a "stability pact" on budgetary discipline in the future euro currency zone.

Chirac pledged to keep on Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who has become the least popular premier in modern French history. A CSA opinion poll released on Wednesday found that 54 percent of French voters want Juppe out.

"I have no intention of making a cabinet reshuffle," he said. Many commentators speculated Chirac he will order a reshuffle sometime next year to streamline the government for elections scheduled in 1998. He praised Juppe as courageous.

Juppe said that Chirac had expressed a great ambition for a strong, generous and united France". Chirac's right-wing allies applauded his performance, before a panel of tough-questioning reporters in the Elysee Palace.
Chirac's only hint of criticism of Juppe was to say that the government should do more to explain its policies better.

"We are a profoundly conservative country where it is extremely difficult to change anything because this runs into traditions, fears and so this is a country that needs a lot of dialogue, explanation," he said.
Serge July of the left-leaning Liberation savaged Chirac in an editorial on Friday for blaming conservatism for France's ills.
"Jacques Chirac has come to tell the French people that it was their fault, that they had no one to blame but themselves. Conservatives the lot of them!" he wrote.

Chirac's only announcement was that he had told the government to set up a commission to reform the judiciary, to strengthen the independence of prosecutors and bolster the presumption of innocence for suspects.

Grilled at length for the first time since he came to office in 1995 about suspected political kickbacks and sleaze probes into political parties including his own, Chirac said: "Probes must be carried out to the end and punishment must be all the more exemplary as it concerns people in position of power."
He also said the government should continue cutting taxes, especially income tax, as part of a fiscal reform. But he also said France should continue "draconian" cuts in spending.
